body:
Reasoning:

* V2 and V3 as well as V51 and V52 also relate to the umbrella concept of "access control"
* "Access control" is a slightly fuzz term
* V4 is primarily around permissions and "Authorization" is an industry standard term to define that.

If we do this, we should replace the use of the phrase "access control" in as many places as possible.

comments.body:
Although I proposed the chapter title update, the task is a bit larger then first thought.

It is also used in 12 requirements, in section titles and in sections texts. All should be updated.

Technically we are talking about access control.

**Authorization:**
This is the process of determining what actions a verified user or system is allowed to perform.

**Access Control:**
Access control is the broader framework that encompasses all the mechanisms—both policies and technical implementations.

Since we are discussing policies and implementations, we are discussing access control.

But I agree the industry is standardizing on Authorization. These terms are really fuzzy the way most people discuss them, but they do have specific meanings.
@jmanico, do you think it is incorrect to say that authentication and session management are aspects of access control?

> [@jmanico](https://github.com/jmanico), do you think it is incorrect to say that authentication and session management are aspects of access control?

Yes. The way I see it described is:

Authentication establishes identity, Access control/Authorization is for feature and data access and session management is the glue between Authentication and Access control/Authorization.

But in general Josh, without being pedantic, I think it's very reasonable to standardize on Authorization. These are terms mostly used in fuzzy ways. OAuth2 is a delegation framework yet they call themselves (incorrectly) authorization.

And PS: Something like re-authentication used to complete a sensitive feature is typically called "step up authorization" to defend a feature yet does not protect a session (since I can go back and keep using the session in most situations). This is typically categorized in access control as opposed to session management. 

My point is, these technologies are very interrelated, but separate layers IMO.
Ok I am going to handle this now
